classification.difficultyReason: Determine the translated reciprocal form from two asymptotes, then use an intercept to determine its coefficient. The third graph requires exact fractional arithmetic.

content.prompt: Find the equation of the following hyperbolas.

spec.sourceRegion: Printed question 20, bottom of the left page column, left graph.
spec.description: Unshaded graph with positive-end axis arrows, two dashed asymptotes and two decreasing blue branches with four continuation arrowheads. The label 3 is above the x-axis and left of its dashed asymptote; −2 is left of the y-axis and above its dashed asymptote; −3 is beside the y-intercept.
spec.mathematics: Vertical asymptote x=3; horizontal asymptote y=−2; y-intercept (0,−3). Reconstructed using y=3/(x−3)−2. The unlabelled x-intercept is retained geometrically. Plot bounds control the illustration and are not additional givens.
spec.answerVisibility: The complete graph and its source labels are permanent question givens. No equation, additional numerical intercept label or origin label is printed.

answer.worked:
The asymptotes are $x=3$ and $y=-2$, so $y=\dfrac{a}{x-3}-2$.

Using the intercept $(0,-3)$:
$$\begin{align*}-3&=\frac{a}{0-3}-2\\-1&=-\frac{a}{3}\\a&=3\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$y=\frac{3}{x-3}-2.$$

answer.worked:
The asymptotes are $x=-3$ and $y=2$, so $y=\dfrac{a}{x+3}+2$.

Using the intercept $(-5,0)$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac{a}{-5+3}+2\\-2&=-\frac{a}{2}\\a&=4\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$y=\frac{4}{x+3}+2.$$

inlines.text: Read the asymptotes, then substitute the origin to find the coefficient.

answer.worked:
The asymptotes are $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $y=\dfrac{5}{2}$, so
$$y=\frac{a}{x+\frac{2}{3}}+\frac{5}{2}.$$
The curve passes through $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac{a}{\frac{2}{3}}+\frac{5}{2}\\-\frac{5}{2}&=\frac{3a}{2}\\a&=-\frac{5}{3}\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{-\frac{5}{3}}{x+\frac{2}{3}}+\frac{5}{2}\\y&=-\frac{5}{3x+2}+\frac{5}{2}.\end{align*}$$
